circles/HistoricalPapers/bell-1964.html.title: J. S. Bell (1964) - On The Einstein Podolski Rosen Paradox
circles/HistoricalPapers/bell-1964.html.html:
J. S. Bell (1964) - On The Einstein Podolski Rosen Paradox

05 August, 2025

Abstract

The paper before us is undoubtedly one of the most important and influential works in the foundations of quantum mechanics. To a large extent, it was written in response to a famous article by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen, in which they argued that quantum mechanics could not be considered a complete theory of physical reality. They suggested the possibility of hidden variables that might explain why quantum mechanics, in their view, only gave an incomplete description of nature.

In his reply, John Bell showed in this groundbreaking article that no theory of hidden variables—at least of the local kind envisioned by Einstein—could reproduce all the predictions of quantum mechanics. Bell’s theorem demonstrated that the structure of quantum theory itself has experimental consequences that cannot be mimicked by any classical hidden-variable model. This established a fundamental test between quantum mechanics and local realism.

In this session, in addition to discussing Bell’s paper, we will examine its historical context and conceptual significance, explaining why it is often regarded as one of the most profound turning points in the philosophy of science and physics. We will also explore the experimental confirmations of Bell’s theorem, as well as the alternative arguments and debates that have emerged in its wake.

Lecturer: Mobin Naderi

circles/HistoricalPapers/born-infeld-193.title: M. Born & L. Infeld (1934) - Foundations of the New Field Theory
circles/HistoricalPapers/born-infeld-193.html:
M. Born & L. Infeld (1934) - Foundations of the New Field Theory

10 June, 2025

Abstract

Born–Infeld electrodynamics is a nonlinear modification of Maxwell’s theory of electromagnetism proposed in the 1930s by Max Born and Leopold Infeld. Its main motivation was to remove the singularities (infinite self-energy) of point charges, such as the infinite energy associated with the electric field of an electron in classical Maxwell theory. The Born–Infeld model introduces an upper bound on the electromagnetic field strength, leading to finite self-energy for point charges. This theory is consistent with special relativity and has reappeared in modern physics, particularly in string theory, where the Born–Infeld action naturally arises in the description of D-branes.

In this session, we will review this paper by Max Born and Leopold Infeld, in which a model of nonlinear electrodynamics is introduced to resolve the singularity problem of point charges. This model, inspired by the idea of an upper limit on velocity in special relativity, imposes an upper bound on electric and magnetic fields. Next, we will examine several issues within the framework of this model, and finally, we will point out the effective role of this model in some aspects of string theory.

Lecturer: Alireza Talebi

circles/HistoricalPapers/chandrasekhar-1.title: S. Chandrasekhar (1931) - The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs
circles/HistoricalPapers/chandrasekhar-1.html:
S. Chandrasekhar (1931) - The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs

14 September, 2025

Abstract

Between 1931 and 1935, the Indian astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar published a series of articles on the stability of stars, in which he introduced the concept of the Chandrasekhar limit for white dwarfs. His work transformed our understanding of stellar structure and opened new windows into the study of stellar evolution. He showed that when the mass of a white dwarf exceeds a certain limit (about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun), electron degeneracy pressure can no longer counterbalance gravity, and the star must collapse into a denser state, leading to the formation of neutron stars or black holes.

In this session, we will become acquainted with the properties of white dwarfs and their evolutionary pathways. We will examine the governing theory of their structure from Chandrasekhar’s perspective, which reshaped our picture of stellar death and revealed why some stars cannot end their lives as white dwarfs. This breakthrough not only gave us a deeper understanding of compact stellar remnants but also explained the fates of massive stars and, eventually, the origins of some of the most extreme objects in the universe.

For this pioneering work, Chandrasekhar was awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics. His studies provided a better understanding of white dwarfs and their ultimate fate, while also paving the way for our comprehension of neutron stars and black holes. In this session, we will also briefly discuss the discovery of pulsars by Jocelyn Bell in 1967, which confirmed the existence of neutron stars and opened a new era in high-energy astrophysics. By exploring how these stellar remnants are structured and how they evolve, we gain a clearer understanding of the processes that shape the life cycles of stars and, ultimately, the cosmos around us.

Lecturer: Bardia Alian

circles/HistoricalPapers/heisenberg-1925.title: W. Heisenberg (1925) - Quantum-Theoretical Re-Interpretation of Kinematic and Mechanical Relations
circles/HistoricalPapers/heisenberg-1925.html:
W. Heisenberg (1925) - Quantum-Theoretical Re-Interpretation of Kinematic and Mechanical Relations

29 July, 2025

Abstract

On July 29, 1925, the young Werner Heisenberg wrote a paper that marked the beginning of a great revolution in physics—an upheaval that set aside the classical concepts of mechanics and motion, and introduced a new world built on matrices, discontinuities, and strange yet precise ideas. Heisenberg’s work, known today as the birth of matrix mechanics, was the first consistent formulation of quantum mechanics. Unlike earlier attempts, it abandoned direct reference to unobservable electron orbits and instead focused only on measurable quantities, such as spectral lines. By representing physical observables as arrays of numbers (matrices) rather than simple numerical values, Heisenberg discovered the non-commutative structure of quantum theory, encapsulated later in the famous commutation relation \( [x, p] = i\hbar \). This marked a decisive shift from the smooth, deterministic picture of classical physics to a probabilistic framework that could accurately capture atomic phenomena.

In this session, on the anniversary of the publication of this paper, we will turn our attention to that exact historical moment—a moment when Heisenberg replaced the comfortable mental images of classical mechanics with something that could not be visualized in the old way. What emerged from his efforts was a new kind of mathematics: matrix mechanics, the earliest form of quantum mechanics, which was later completed and expanded by the works of Born and Jordan.

Lecturer: Sohrab Maleki

circles/HistoricalPapers/planck-1900.htm.html:
M. Planck (1900) - On the Theory of the Energy Distribution Law of the Normal Spectrum

09 March, 2025

Abstract

At the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth, discrepancies were observed between experimental results and theoretical predictions based on classical physics. One such inconsistency was the problem of black-body radiation. While the total radiative power of a black body could be described using thermodynamic considerations, the frequency distribution of that radiation conflicted with theoretical expectations. In 1900, Max Planck proposed a hypothesis that required energy to be quantized, offering a solution for the frequency distribution of black-body radiation that agreed closely with experimental data. This achievement is regarded as a cornerstone of quantum physics.

In this session, we will review the historical background and analyze the content of Planck’s paper with the very question of "How did Planck come up with this strange idea?!".

Lecturer: Sohrab Maleki

circles/Phys&Math/computational-neurosci.title: Computational Neuroscience
circles/Phys&Math/computational-neurosci.html:
Computational Neuroscience

Lecturer: Ashkan Damavandi

Computational neuroscience is an interdisciplinary field that combines physiology and neurobiology, physics, mathematics, and computer science to understand and analyze the mechanisms of the brain. By using data analysis, mathematical modeling, and simulation methods, this field examines processes of the brain at multiple scales—from the dynamics of individual neurons and synapses to emergent behaviors of neural networks such as decision-making, environmental adaptation, and sensory processing.

In this study circle, we will proceed step by step, starting from basic and introductory topics, to become familiar with modeling and simulation tools in computational neuroscience. Given the breadth and depth of the field, we will devote extra time to more important topics when necessary in order to maximize learning and effectiveness.


References: Computational neuroscience encompasses a wide range of topics, each with its own significance. As such, a single comprehensive reference that adequately covers all areas is either insufficient or rarely available. Therefore, throughout the circle we will use and introduce different sources for different topics. We will begin with two main books: Dynamical Systems in Neuroscience by Izhikevich and Neuronal Dynamics by Gerstner. In addition to textbooks and lecture notes, we will also review a variety of reputable research papers.


Prerequisites: Biological and physiological aspects of neuroscience—such as biochemical mechanisms of the nervous system and the function of neurons—will be introduced as needed during the sessions. Therefore, prior knowledge in these areas is not required. For better engagement with the material, minimal familiarity with differential equations, basic probability, general physics, and introductory Python programming is very useful. In addition, a general background in statistical mechanics and linear algebra can be helpful. However, whenever necessary, we will provide quick reviews of prerequisites and recommend supplementary resources.

Sessions

0. Introduction to the Study Circle

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 30 July 2025

1. Single-Neuron models (I)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 02 August 2025

3. Mathematical Foundations of modelling in Neuroscience (II)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 13 August 2025

The Hodgkin–Huxley and Morris–Lecar models examine the role of ion channels in neuronal membranes and their effect on changes in the membrane’s electrical potential. The Pinsky–Rinzel model studies neural spikes in the soma and dendrite of pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus, the Kuramoto model addresses the collective activity of neurons, and the Wilson–Cowan model investigates the interactions between populations of neurons. In this session, we will continue exploring concepts of dynamical systems using these models.

  • Analysis of attractors, equilibrium, and chaotic behavior in the Hodgkin–Huxley and Pinsky–Rinzel models
  • Stability and equilibrium in the Kuramoto phase model
  • Lyapunov function and exponent in the LIF model

In the upcoming sessions of the circle, we will begin examining epilepsy as an important case study for modeling neural networks. In computational neuroscience, models must be validated and checked for accuracy by comparing their results with electrophysiological data. One type of data commonly used for this purpose is EEG.

In this session, after introducing epilepsy and EEG data, we will move on to comparing and analyzing the results of the Wilson–Cowan and Jansen–Rit models. Finally, we will discuss the importance of stochastic fluctuations and noise in modeling, as a way to achieve better agreement with real-world data.

circles/Phys&Math/em-in-gr.html.title: The Theory of Electrodynamics in General Relativity
circles/Phys&Math/em-in-gr.html.html:
The Theory of Electrodynamics in General Relativity

Conductor: Mobin Naderi


The presentation of this circle will unfold in two acts. We begin by outlining the path of the sessions.

Act I: We will first develop tensor calculus alongside special relativity, and then build up to general relativity and its mathematics at the level of tensor analysis. Electromagnetism will be reformulated in covariant form and expressed in the language of both special and general relativity. Finally, we will derive Einstein’s field equations and their electro-vacuum solution.

Act II: The mathematics employed in the first act requires further refinement. We will therefore revisit the notions of tensors, metrics, and related concepts. Beginning with linear algebra, we will introduce the basics of topological spaces and then move on to manifolds, since Einstein’s equivalence principle naturally calls for a formulation in the language of manifolds. With differential forms in hand, we will return to Maxwell’s equations and construct their geometric form. Ultimately, we will explore derivatives in relativity more carefully, which will allow us to discuss spacetime symmetries. Building on this, we will linearize Einstein’s equations and, using spacetime symmetries, introduce gravitational waves.

In summary, our goal is to restate everything presented in Act I in tensorial language, but this time fully within the framework of differential geometry.


Reference:The sources for this circle are broad and varied, but the main references will be shared in the study group.


Prerequisites:We will try to cover the essential prerequisites throughout the sessions themselves. However, prior familiarity with classical electromagnetism and linear algebra is required.

  • Some Tensor Identities

circles/Phys&Math/intro-quantum.html.html:
Introduction to Quantum Mechanics

Conductor: Zahra Amiri


In this circle, we will study and learn quantum mechanics from the ground up. The goal is to make sure that even participants who do not have prior familiarity with the subject can gradually become acquainted with quantum mechanics. The sessions will begin with fundamental topics and will roughly cover the equivalent of Quantum Mechanics I and II at the university level.

Unlike most of the ongoing Quanta circles, our intention here is to make this circle more interactive, with presentations given by physics students themselves.

Presenters do not need prior knowledge of quantum mechanics; simply reading the section they are assigned, along with reviewing previous material, will be sufficient. During their presentation, they can also ask questions that arose for them, clarify points, share additional insights, and engage in Q&A. These discussions will be complemented by the session organizer and other students who have studied more deeply.

The topics of the circle will follow the order in the table of contents of the main reference, but we may also incorporate material from other sources. All announcements about the circle will be made in the group


Reference:The primary text we will follow is Introduction to Quantum Mechanics by David Griffiths — a clear and accessible book for beginning this subject. We will also have dedicated problem-solving sessions, where we will work through interesting or challenging exercises from Griffiths or questions drawn from elsewhere.

circles/Phys&Math/kinetic-theory.html.title: Kinetic Theory
circles/Phys&Math/kinetic-theory.html.html:
Kinetic Theory

Lecturer: Sohrab Maleki

Kinetic Theory is a comprehensive study circle exploring the statistical description of many-particle systems. Across this circle we discuss the foundations of statistical mechanics, the derivation of transport equations and the emergent behaviours of gases, plasmas and beyond. Through lectures, readings and open discussions we build up the BBGKY hierarchy, derive Boltzmann’s equation and analyse non-equilibrium phenomena. Whether you are new to the field or looking to solidify your understanding, join us as we probe the microscopic underpinnings of macroscopic physics.

Sessions

1. Elementary Kinetic Theory

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 16 March 2025

In this lecture, I start the investigating elementary kinetic theory. I obtain the so-called Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and then, delve into calculating cool properties of matter assuming thermal equilibrium.

Recording Notes

2. Transport Phenomena

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 19 March 2025

In this lecture, I investigate the Transport Phenomena. I begin with the mean free path; Then I turn to the Random Walk problem and consequently express the diffusion, fomulate the viscosity and finally, thermal conductivity using elementary kinetic theory methods. This session was the end of "Elementary Kinetic Theory" topic.

Recording Notes

3. A Review on Classical Mechanics

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 23 March 2025

In this lecture, I review classical mechanics (and a bit of thermodynamics). This builds a comprehensive mathematical structure to beginning the treatment with the dynamics of many body systems (what we aim to reach in kinetic theory).

Recording Notes

4. The BBGKY Hierarchy

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 25 March 2025

This lecture is the start of the advanced kinetic theory. In this lecture, I begin with Liouville's equation and formulate the BBGKY hierarchy. Although, as we show, it doesn't make life any easier than Liouville's equation, It's the way we reformulate the general problem in a way that is comprehensive for approximation methods.

Recording Notes

5. Boltzmann's Equation (1)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 27 March 2025

In this lecture, I begin the investigation of Boltzmann's equation. In this series of sessions, we cover two approaches to Boltzmann's equation: A more easy-going approach and another more rigorous way. In this lecture, we cover the first approach. Throughout the investigations, we would be relied on Boltzmann's equation for many purposes.

Recording Notes

6. Boltzmann's Equation (2)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 30 March 2025

In this lecture, I begin to discuss detailed balance condition and how the collision integral is the tendacy of the many body system to Boltzmann distribution by producing the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for an ideal gas. Then, I turn into the Quantum version of Boltzmann equation and finally investigate a better derivation of Boltzmnann equation starting from the BBGKY hierarchy.

Recording Notes

7. H-Theorem (& the first look to fluid dynamics)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 01 April 2025

In this lecture, I'd derive and discuss the so-called H-Theorem originally derived by L. Boltzmann. I demonstrate how the "molecular chaos" assumption is the key to irreversibility. Then I turn to general discussions about Fluid Dynamics, introduce collisional invariants and derive the master equation governing slow-varying quantities time evolution. There's also a recommended reading for this session: Violation of Boltzmann's H-Theorem in Real Gases.

Recording Notes

8. The Ideal Fluid

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 03 April 2025

In this lecture, I discuss the equations of motion in a fluid using the master equation derived for slow-varying quantities in the previous lecture. I show that these are not sufficient in determining the fluid properties. Then, I introduce the ideal fluid, extract its equations of evolution and show they miss dissipation. Then I demonstrate why.

Recording Notes

9. The Dissipation & Viscous Fluid

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 06 April 2025

This is the last lecture of the Kinetic Theory study circle. As we saw in the previous lecture, the ideal fluid misses dissipation (and therefore equilibrium). In this lecture I investigate how to include dissipation (through relaxation time approximation) and treat thermal conductivity and viscosity according to it. Finally, I'd derive the so-called Navier-Stokes equations governing the motion of viscous fluid.

Recording Notes

circles/Phys&Math/quantum-field-theory.h.title: Quantum Field Theory
circles/Phys&Math/quantum-field-theory.h.html:
Quantum Field Theory

Lecturer: Mohammad Amin Sadeghian

In this study circle, we aim for a deeper and more fundamental perspective on Quantum Field Theory (QFT), both from the physical and the mathematical standpoint. Quantum Field Theory is an extensive field with a wide range of topics, where even a thorough examination of a single subject can take months or years. Nevertheless, in the standard way it is usually taught, many important aspects are presented without sufficient depth and richness. This often leads to serious difficulties in building the necessary foundation for understanding more modern and advanced areas of physics. Taking this limitation into account, we will begin with the basics and gradually move toward more advanced and contemporary topics in field theory. Whenever we feel that a discussion or topic requires deeper reflection, we will refer to additional sources and papers. However, in order to avoid excessive perfectionism and unnecessary slowdown, we will follow one or at most two main textbooks as our primary references and framework.


References: From the physical perspective, the circle’s main reference will be Fradkin’s book. Its strength lies in its effort to provide a comprehensive picture of field theory as a framework applied throughout physics—not only in the standard computations of scattering amplitudes and Feynman diagrams for elementary particles, but also in shaping the physicist’s broader intuition. From the mathematical perspective, the references will be either Talagrand or Hamilton, with the relative weight depending on how much mathematical emphasis the circle chooses to pursue.


Prerequisites: Participants are expected to be familiar with Quantum Mechanics, Special Relativity, and to some extent Classical Field Theory. A brief and preliminary familiarity with Quantum Field Theory would also be helpful in following the sessions, though it is not strictly required.

circles/Phys&Math/quantum-theory.html.html:
Quantum Theory

Lecturer: Sohrab Maleki


Quantum Theory is a study circle in which covered a brief review on the pragmatic meaning and an extensive discussion on foundations of quantum mechanics. It is desired to entirely cover the topics of a book written by Asher Peres. Here's the content I wish to cover by the end of the circle:


Part I: *Introduction to Quantum Physics *Quantum Tests *Complex Vector Space *Continuous Variables

Part II: *Composite Systems *Bell's Theorem *Contextuality

Part III: *Space-time Symmetries *Information and Thermodynamics *Semiclassical Methods *Chaos and Irreversibility *Measuring Process.


You can also see the playlist of these set of lectures in lecturer's youtube channel.

Sessions

Part I: Gathering The Tools

1. Introduction to Quantum Theory

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 07 July 2025

In this lecture, I talked first about the purpose, preliminaries, mathematical level, etc., the general layout of the study circle and begun the introduction to quantum theory. This is done by considering quantum phenomena of light.

Recording Slides

2. Quantum Tests (I)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 09 July 2025

In this lecture, I've completed the "Introduction to Quantum Physics" and have defined the primitive notions of quantum theory. Here, I defined the primitive concepts "Preperations" and "Tests" which can not be defined in term of more primitive notions. Then I defined Quantum Systems, Quantum States, Repeatable Tests and Maximal tests.

3. Quantum Tests (II)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 13 July 2025

In this lecture, I've discussed the interference postulate and its necessity in order to make the theory self-consistent. Then, formulated only the "experimental observations" and showed how matrices (and linear algebra as a whole) are well candidates for being used to formulate the theory. Transition amplitudes are defined and "chosen" to form unitary matrices (using the phase/gauge freedom). Up to now, nothing has came out of nowhere (and no wavefunction or state "vectors" have been defined or postulated). In next session, We use the advantage of linear algebra and define all these mathematical objects for convenience.

Recording Slides

4. Complex Vector Space (I)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 16 July 2025

In this lecture, I've discussed the Idea of construction of a vector space for which these matrices act on. It wasn't held online due to technical difficulties but its contents will be recorded.

5. Complex Vector Space (II)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 20 July 2025

In this lecture, I've discussed the determination of the transition amplitudes in simple cases (in principle, from experimental data) and mathematical treatment of observables.

Recording Notes

6. Continuous Variables (I)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 23 July 2025

In this lecture, I've ended the fomulation of Quantum Theory of a quantum system by formulating the quantum mixtures using density matrix and investing its properties (and show how it is evaluated in practice). Then, I've began ``Continuous Variables"; This is not a complete, mathematically complete investigation of continuous spectra from mathematical zero point. But we mention some common issues appear (with physical consequence) if one ignores mathematical rigor. In this lecture, I've shown some difficulties of generalization of finite-dimensional matrices to infinite dimensions and discussed strong and weak convergence.

Recording Notes

7. Continuous Variables (II)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 27 July 2025

In this lecture, I've briefly reviewed the notion of ``propagators" because of its application (we'd back to this in chapters related to quantum dynamics) and showed that Hilbert space unavoidably contains discontinuous wavefunctions. We've actually shown that the Schrodinger equation itself, can evolve a continuous, differentiable, square-integrable function into a discontinuous one! then talked about the notion of ``separability" of a Hilbert space briefly (because quantum mechanics doesn't have to do anything with this. The relevant difficulties arise when dealing with quantization of fields).

Recording Notes

8. Continuous Variables (III)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 31 July 2025

In this lecture, I've discussed linear operators. I begun by showing that how some innocent-looking finite-dimensional matrices cannot make sense when generalized to infinite dimensions and motivated the ``Domain of Definition" and ``Boundedness" of an operator. Then, defined adjoint operation and the notions of ``Self-Adjoint" & ``Symmetric" operators (and their difference!). Then, I show that momentum operator is not symmetric nor self-adjoint when defined on a finite region! unless it is defined on certain functions satisfying a boundary conditions.

Recording Notes

9. Continuous Variables (IV)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 02 August 2025

In this lecture, I've shown that it is possible to upgrade some symmetric operators to self-adjoint ones by expanding their domain of defitnition through an example (momentum operator in finite region). Then investigated their physical significance and how their show-up in Aharonov-Bohm effect. Then, I've shown that this is not always possible (with a simple counter example: radial momentum) and some symmetric operators cannot become self-adjoint in any ways! Now, we've delved into uncertainty relations. I've reviewed the formal derivation of them to be aware of mathematical assumptions behind each step for futher investigations.

Recording Notes

10. Continuous Variables (V)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 06 August 2025

In this lecture, I show how the ``minimum uncertainty" state can be derived and show that this is the cohearent state for momentum and position uncertainty. Then show that there's no such an uncertainty between angular momentum and angle operators because the mathematical assumptions in deriving uncertainty relations do not hold in this case. Then I show other difficulties arised by continuous spectra in commutation relations. Finally, I show that continuous operators do not have eigenvectors at all! but since we've defined measurements outcomes as eigenvectors, this is a serious difficulty that must be resolved. I've introduced the method which ``truncates'' the Hilbert space in order to approximamte the actual infinite-dimensional Hilbert space by a finite-dimensional one (which doesn't have such difficulties). But it will turn out that trunction method (which is notably successful in chemical physics), has unfortunate results and cannot be considered as an appropriate way to deal with continuous variables.

Recording Notes

11. Continuous Variables (VI)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 12 August 2025

In this lecture, I've introduced the ``Spectral Theory" as the appropriate treatment of continuous spectra and explore in detail the method.

Recording Notes

Part II: Quantum Inseparability, Nonlocality & Contextuality

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 14 August 2025

13. Composite Systems (II)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 19 August 2025

In this lecture, I've showed how quantum systems can be decorrelated and demonstrated how it is possible to construct a quantum test with an entangled state in its basis and shown how to treat experimental errors in measuring instruments in this case.

Recording Notes

14. Composite Systems (III)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 09 September 2025

In this lecture, I've shown how it is possible to find the state of each subsystem individually if we know the state of the composite system and likewise, why it is impossible to do the vice-versa (i.e. to find the state of composite system based on the states of its subsystems). I've introduced incomplete tests and partial traces to aim this.

Recording Notes

15. Composite Systems (IV)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 11 September 2025

In this lecture, I've completed the mathematical treatment of composite systems by introducing the Schmidt decomposition. I've shown how this decomposition is possible for a composite system made out of two subsystems and how it is equivalent to diagonalize the reduced density matrices of subsystems. I also started the discussion of identical particles and motivated the Bosons and Fermions classification.

Recording Notes

16. Composite Systems (V)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 13 September 2025

In this lecture, I've written down the Fermionic and Bosonic Hilbert spaces and pointed out that these particles are "necessarily entangled" as an obvious consequence of their identical nature; even if they're prepared independently. Then, I've investigated the question of "Cluster Separability". In other words, I've investigated if this entanglement is a matter concern? I've shown that if these particles are far enough (with a proper mathematical definition of "far enough"), although they're still entangled, this entanglement doesn't influence any observable. This question which is answer easily in this case, will play a fundamental role when we investigate the systems with more than two particles which additional, non-trivial symmetries appear.

Recording Notes

17. Composite Systems (VI)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 18 September 2025

In this lecture, I've introduced "Parastatistics and tried to find all symmetric bases in the Hilbert space of 3 identical particles. Two of this bases are abviously Bosonic and Fermionic bases. I've shown that there are other 4 symmetric bases and found them with aid of Group Theory. This group is actually called "symmetric group". I've introduced it and found those bases. Therefore, it seems that there are particles other than Fermions and Bosons (?!). I'll resolve this issue in the next session showing that these new bases are "unlikely" due to cluster inseparability.

Notes

18. Composite Systems (VII)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 21 September 2025

In this lecture, I take the generalized "identical particles states" found in the previous lecture and show that they are experimentally distinguishable. Further, I show that all the states except Fermionic / Bosonic ones violate the cluster separability (i.e. when one of three states is "far away", the observables do not reduce to those of two particles). This reasoning, demonstrates the difficulties of existence of something rather than Fermions and Bosons (although it doesn't disprove their existence. It's just about them being "unlikely").

Notes

19. Composite Systems (VIII)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 23 September 2025

In this lecture, I discuss the following misconception: "We know that two fermions (like a hydrogen atom made of a proton and a neutron) behaves like a boson. But bosons can occupy the same state. How is it possible that two hydrogen atoms get in the same state while their electrons and protons cannot get into the same state?" I demonistrate this issue through an example and show the necessary approximations and conditions fot this to happen. Then, I begin the introduction to Fock Space and occupation number representation.

Notes

20. Composite Systems (IX)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 03 October 2025

In this lecture, I introduce the creation & annihilation operators and show their (anti-) commutation relations.

Notes

21. Composite Systems (X)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 03 October 2025

In this lecture, I introduce the so-called "Second Quantization" and show how single-particle and two-particle operators can be written in term of creation/annihilation operators and have no reference to the total number of particles.

Notes

Solid State Physics

Conductor: Abolfazl Mahdaei


In this circle, we will study and learn solid state physics. The goal is to become familiar with and acquire the basic foundations necessary for the condensed matter physics track. We will also make use of prior knowledge from quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics, allowing us to see more clearly how these subjects find application in condensed matter systems. The sessions will start from fundamental topics and will roughly cover the equivalent of Solid State Physics I as taught in universities.

This circle will also be interactive: interested students will present different sections of the book in each session. Further details about the format, presentations, and references will be given in the introductory “session zero.”

The topics of the circle will follow the order of the table of contents of the main reference book, but we may also bring in material from other sources. Any changes or updates will be announced in the group:


Reference:The primary text we will follow is Oxford Solid State Basics by Steven Simon — a clear and accessible book for beginning this subject. As mentioned, additional material will occasionally be drawn from other sources, such as David Tong’s lecture notes. Supplementary resources will also be shared in the group. We will also have problem-solving sessions, where we will work through exercises together.

circles/Phys&Math/stochastic-processes.h.title: Stochastic Processes
circles/Phys&Math/stochastic-processes.h.html:
Stochastic Processes

Lecturer: Hooman Zare

“The gap between physical intuition and mathematical rigor is where demons hide.” — Hermann Weyl


Stochastic (or random) processes are one of those fields where mathematics and physics are forced to advance only by helping one another. In such contexts, Hermann Weyl’s warning is often the most central and most difficult part of the story. Therefore, the aim of these sessions is to take a closer look at situations where our physical intuition might mislead us.

In these meetings, we will begin by exploring both the traditional and newer intuitions surrounding these processes, and use them to introduce the topic from an interdisciplinary perspective. Then, we will tackle a number of modern problems, and finally turn to problems that we once thought we had solved—or still think we have solved correctly—and show how experiments, computer simulations, relations, and even laws can break down! Afterwards, with the insights we have gained, we will attempt to formulate research directions that can push open problems a step further.


References: Stochastic processes are both extremely detailed and, at the same time, highly reducible. For this reason, references may range from undergraduate physics texts to books in pure mathematics; thus, the best approach is to learn “on demand.” However, if you wish to pursue research in this area from an applied perspective, it is recommended to use a comprehensive book that does not follow a strict proof-based style yet is far from simplistic. One of the best books that follows such an approach is Dr. Rahimi Tabar’s Analysis and Data-Based Reconstruction of Complex Nonlinear Dynamical Systems.


Prerequisites: Since most prerequisites for these discussions are not part of the standard curriculum, they will be addressed within the sessions themselves. Familiarity with statistics and probability, as well as general ideas about entropy, partition functions, and Brownian motion, can be helpful. Overall, the most important skill required is the ability to follow the discussion—even when the details are not entirely clear!

Sessions

0. Introduction to the Study Circle

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 25 July 2025

1. An Introduction to Stochastic Processes

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 28 July 2025

Building on the previous session, in this circle we will begin with a distribution function, construct stochastic processes based on known statistics, and then introduce one of the most famous and powerful tools of discrete stochastic systems: the Master equation. Using this tool, we can solve many modern problems and study well-known papers across various fields.

The core concepts of this session will be stationarity tests, the Master equation, and its equivalents in other disciplines (for example: Fermi levels, the Lindblad equation for open quantum systems, chemical reaction equations, gene expression equations, reduced density matrices in cosmological fields, SIR and population models, the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation in control theory, agent-based modeling, hidden states in CTMCs in computer science, Redfield relaxation theory in spin resonance, Förster/Dexter transfer in condensed matter physics, and more).

After proving the theorems, we will try to examine these examples in detail and learn the main idea of how the Master equation is applied in each of these fields. Finally, by introducing a curious example of a chemical balance that created major challenges in dynamical systems, we will put this theory to the test, solve it, and eliminate one of the common assumptions usually made in solving any Master equation.

For this session, the following concepts are required, but they will not be introduced in detail. If needed, it is recommended to consult the relevant Wikipedia pages or use AI assistance:

  1. Matrix calculus.
  2. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
  3. Solving the equation dx/dt = Ax, where A is a matrix and x a vector.
  4. Commutators and anticommutators.
  5. Derivative, partial derivative, integral.
  6. Dirac delta, its integral, and its cumulative distribution function.
Notes

2. The Master Equation

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 01 August 2025

One of the key tools in studying systems with a large number of agents is the Master equation, which describes the evolution of the probability distribution of the entire system’s state. This equation finds applications across many domains, from statistical physics to economics; however, in this session, the focus will be on its role in modeling games with many players and in reinforcement learning.

On the other hand, the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation lies at the heart of optimal control methods. By describing the value function of a decision-making policy, it enables finding the optimal trajectory for each agent. In stochastic environments and multi-agent games, combining the HJB framework with mean-field approaches leads to an extended Master equation, which guides decision optimization at the population level.

To make these concepts more tangible, we will consider a simple example of the Snakes and Ladders game. In the classical version, a player’s movement is determined solely by the dice; but once decision-making is introduced, the problem changes entirely.

Exercise: You can write a program that, by calculating probabilities, determines from each square of Snakes and Ladders the average number of dice rolls required to finish the game. Independently, you can simulate 1,000 runs of the game and observe the statistics; then extend this number to 1,000,000 runs to see how the averages behave.

Notes

3. The Control of Stochastic and Non-Stochastic Systems

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 08 August 2025

  • Solving the Snakes and Ladders problem with decision-making
  • Matrix properties of the Master equation
  • Introduction to Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) control
  • Extending the Master equation to continuous systems
Notes

4. The Control of Stochastic Systems (II)

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 11 August 2025

  • The viscosity method for non-trivial equations
  • Suitable conditions for approximating the solution of a stochastic equation
  • Variation methods for stochastic problems
  • Forward and backward stochastic partial differential equations
  • Solvability of a stochastic equation
  • Control of nonlinear systems
Notes

5. Measure Theory and Statistics

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 15 August 2025

In this session, we will focus on the mathematical foundations of stochastic analysis and the theory of stochastic processes. The goal is to make all definitions precise, introduce the key concepts, and prove some of the well-known theorems in this area.

This session is primarily aimed at pure mathematics students or those with a strong interest in these topics, since—unlike the previous sessions—most of the discussion will be devoted to analysis, measure theory, and set theory.

Notes

6. The Equation of Motion and Stochastic Probability Equation

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 18 August 2025

  • Categorization of all random motions
  • Introduction of the differential equation governing the probability distribution of random motions
  • Derivation of the Kramers–Moyal equation from the definition of the Markov property
  • Introduction to the continuous subset of the Kramers–Moyal equation (Fokker–Planck)
  • Introduction and derivation of the differential equation of random motion (Langevin)

7. Continuous Stochastic Analysis

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 22 August 2025

  • Ito Integral

8. Stochastic Integration

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 12 September 2025

  • Itô integral
  • Martingale
  • Limit of stochastic sequences
Notes

9. Martingale

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 19 September 2025

  • Stopping time
  • Doob's theorem
  • Martingale representation theorem
  • Quadratic variation and predictable compensator
Notes

10. Multi-Dimensional Stochastic Processes

Quanta Study Circles, SUT – 22 September 2025

  • Linear & Non-Linear Interactions

circles/SpecialTopics/1-rangriz.html.title: Scaling Limits: Effective Dynamics Vs. Dynamical Mean-Field Theory
circles/SpecialTopics/1-rangriz.html.html:
Scaling Limits: Effective Dynamics Vs. Dynamical Mean-Field Theory

05 July, 2025

Abstract

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a key algorithm for training neural networks, yet its success in complex, high-dimensional settings is not fully understood. Tools from the statistical physics of disordered systems (spin glasses), especially Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT), offer insight by approximating the dynamics of learning. In this thesis, we show that DMFT fails to capture crucial fluctuation effects near saddle points, in what's known as the diffusive regime. There, SGD behaves via a stochastic differential equation (SDE), something DMFT does not account for. This highlights the limits of mean-field approaches and the importance of the effective dynamics using the information exponent in high-dimensional learning.

Lecturer: Parsa Rangriz

Mathematics PhD Student @ UC San Diego

circles/SpecialTopics/2-sadri.html.title: Quasi Inversion of Quantum & Classical Channels in Finite Dimensions
circles/SpecialTopics/2-sadri.html.html:
Quasi Inversion of Quantum & Classical Channels in Finite Dimensions

10 August, 2025

Abstract

In closed quantum systems, the evolution of states under the Schrödinger equation is fully reversible — meaning one can return exactly to the past. However, if the system is open and interacts with its surroundings, then without complete control over the environment, exact reversal becomes impossible. How are these non-unitary evolutions, also known as “quantum channels,” described? If we cannot completely eliminate environmental noise, to what extent can we bring the system “close” to its initial state again? And more importantly, what answers does the classical version of these questions offer, and what similarities or differences emerge compared to the quantum case? In this week’s “Quanta,” I will present a brief overview of my and my colleagues’ efforts to find answers to these questions.

Lecturer: Koorosh Sadri

Physics PhD Student @ Penn. State University

About Quanta

Quanta is a student‑led initiative originated at the Sharif University of Technology that organises open study circles to explore the depth and breadth of physics. Our aim is to create a collaborative environment where students and enthusiasts can learn, discuss and teach each other topics ranging from historical breakthroughs to contemporary research.


We host a variety of circles. They're organized into three main classes: Mathematics & Physics, Historical Papers and Special Topics. Each circle features lectures, discussions and resources curated by passionate organisers. Whether you're just starting your physics journey or seeking a deeper understanding, Quanta welcomes you.


Guide on Study Circles

Physics & Mathematics: These set of circles are dedicated to study some well-known topics on physics and mathematics. Their purpose varies from introduction of the topic to others (especially courses we lack at SUT), getting a deeper understanding of the topic, delve more into mathematical details, etc. This is where students discuss and learn a topic together.


Historical Papers: These sessions are dedicated to read and review the groundbreaking, usually old papers from great minds of physics in the history. The aim is understanding the idea, environment and the paradigm of their thinking which has led to these breakthrough discoveries.


Special Topics: These sessions are dedicated to little-known, relatively advanced topics and modern papers that worth investigating together.
